deep_why: MiniAMIE computes inference rules from knowledge graphs, the core challenge being that exhaustively checking all possible rules becomes infeasible as the search space grows exponentially. The soundness rests on restricted search—by excluding less productive rule patterns upfront and using rapid estimates for rule quality metrics instead of exact counts, the method trades completeness for speed while keeping found rules reliable. This works because rule metrics follow predictable patterns in real graphs: a rule's overall strength can be approximated from a smaller sample without distorting which rules genuinely matter. The payoff is dramatic speedup on massive graphs while still harvesting good-quality rules that capture meaningful relationships, making knowledge graph analysis tractable for large modern systems.

CS2NET estimates platform-wide revenue lift from adding inventory, the core quantity being whether a single inventory addition truly increases total sales or merely shifts bookings between hotels. Standard approaches fail because adding a room invites selection bias: hotels that accept the added inventory differ systematically from those that refuse. The method enforces causal reasoning by measuring what would have happened without the intervention, using scarcity and service patterns to correct for this bias. This works because scarcity and hotel acceptance follow learnable patterns tied to real availability and service quality—once those are known, the algorithm can identify comparable inventory scenarios and isolate the causal effect from confounding. The result is trustworthy measurement of genuine platform uplift, not misleading tallies of shifted sales, enabling profitable operational decisions.

PC-SAD identifies groups of anomalous nodes in graphs, not just individual odd nodes, where the core task is recognizing when a cluster of nodes behaves abnormally as a unified pattern. The approach combines two complementary signals: first, it identifies suspicious nodes by examining their local neighborhoods at multiple scales, then it amplifies the collaborative patterns among candidate subgraphs by contrasting normal structures against anomalies. This works because anomalous subgraphs show coherent internal structure that differs markedly from typical neighborhoods—by learning what normal collaboration looks like across many subgraph shapes, the system can recognize when a group's internal cohesion deviates from expectation. The payoff is detecting fraud rings or compromised clusters that a node-centric view would miss, catching organized anomalies rather than isolated misbehavior.

CASE updates an LLM's knowledge through targeted edits to internal neurons, the core challenge being that making one edit can silently break unrelated factual knowledge or conflict with previous edits. Rather than applying edits arbitrarily, CASE first quantifies conflicts between new knowledge and prior edits, then selects specific neurons whose learned features are most connected to the knowledge being updated. This works because neural knowledge is not uniformly distributed—most facts are encoded redundantly across many neurons, but some neurons are specializing in exactly the domain being edited, and those are safest to update. By assessing conflicts upfront and targeting sensitive neurons, the method preserves older knowledge while installing new facts, avoiding cascading forgetting that plagued prior systems. Scaling to thousands of sequential edits becomes feasible because conflicts are resolved before they damage the whole model.

Meteor delivers control commands through virtual cloud infrastructure, where the core challenge is choosing between two fundamentally different transport paths: direct peer-to-peer calls (fast but overload the sending side) or message queues (overload the receiving side but more reliable). The system automatically switches between them, choosing RPC when the network is lightly loaded and queues when the network is saturated. This works because the two bottlenecks do not saturate together—when sender capacity is exhausted, queues still have room to absorb messages, and vice versa. By monitoring which resource is scarcer and switching to use the other path, the system always steers traffic where it flows least resistively, minimizing delays. The result is that millions of commands reliably reach thousands of nodes with minimal wait, something neither pure RPC nor pure queueing achieves alone.

Post-quantum cryptography migration prioritizes which cryptographic components in blockchains and decentralized systems must update first to resist quantum attacks. The method builds a taxonomy mapping each component (key agreement, signatures, verification) and their dependencies, then applies priority rules derived from which components, if broken by a quantum adversary, would compromise the most downstream operations. This works because decentralized systems have long-lived public records and governance constraints—upgrading in the wrong order either breaks backward compatibility or leaves vulnerabilities exposed during transition. By inventorying all cryptographic dependencies explicitly and using dependency depth as the priority signal, the framework ensures that the most critical paths (e.g., wallet signing) upgrade before peripheral ones, minimizing interoperability fractures. The payoff is a principled migration roadmap without expensive trial deployments.

This work measures human ability to detect AI-generated news versus real content, the core question being whether improved language models have outpaced human perception and defenses. The authors built controlled tools—one to generate synthetic news and another to gather human judgments—so they can run fair side-by-side comparisons. This works because detection is a discernible signal if you can hold all other variables constant: show humans real and fake news generated by the same system, measure detection rates, and repeat as AI improves. By instrumenting both generation and human perception, they avoid confounding factors and isolate genuine progress in the generation-versus-detection race. The finding—that detection is improving but remains a competitive arms race—informs realistic risk models for misinformation ecosystems and points to hybrid defenses beyond pure detection.

This work detects overlapping communities in temporal social networks enriched with psycholinguistic signals like grievances and moral framings, the core question being whether adding semantic meaning (what people express emotionally and ethically) sharpens community detection beyond raw interaction patterns alone. The method layers psycholinguistic attributes alongside interaction edges, then applies community detection that respects both layers. This works because real communities often bond through shared moral reasoning and emotional expression, not just who talks to whom—adding these as explicit network layers provides additional constraints that separate loosely connected groups into tighter, more meaningful clusters. By measuring community cohesion and temporal persistence with and without semantic layers, the authors show that expressing values creates stronger structural signal than interaction alone. The payoff is communities that reflect genuine solidarity and aligned belief, not spurious groupings based on conversation frequency.

SparseCTR predicts click-through rates by learning sparse attention over long sequences of user behavior, the core computation being which past behaviors matter most for predicting the next action when sequence length explodes. Standard attention scales quadratically with sequence length (checking all past behaviors against the present), making it infeasible for years of user history. The method segments behaviors into chunks in a way that respects each user's natural rhythm—avoiding artificial breaks in continuous activities—then applies three sparse attention branches to capture global interests, shifts in interest, and recent impulses. This works because user behavior exhibits strong temporal locality and personal pacing: most influence comes from recent actions, occasional surges in interest, and long-term preferences, not every single past interaction. By pruning to these structured patterns and learning which users emphasize which branches, the system reduces attention cost from quadratic to nearly linear while improving predictions. The result is tractable modeling of multiyear behavior sequences in production systems.

This paper balances efficiency (maximizing value gained) and fairness (ensuring no agent is drastically worse off) when assigning items to agents whose value depends on which position they hold, with the added constraint that each item can only go to specific positions. The core challenge is that fairness demands checking every agent's satisfaction, yet efficiency demands maximizing total value—these objectives can conflict. The method characterizes which combinations are feasible by solving for the approximation ratio between the best fair allocation and the best efficient allocation. This works because optimal assignments in constrained position-based allocation follow predictable trade-off curves: the method computes bounds showing when fairness can be achieved cheaply and when it requires real sacrifice. By working through the computational complexity first, the authors provide algorithms that guarantee either fairness or efficiency (or approximate both), depending on the constraint graph structure. The payoff is principled guidance for real allocation problems where positions matter—e.g., assigning research projects to qualified staff—balancing worker satisfaction against organizational goals.

MASI runs spiking neural networks on tiny embedded devices, where the core challenge is that SNNs require recomputing state over many timesteps, each timestep demanding memory to hold intermediate activations. The method adapts layer-wise memory usage on the fly: as available RAM shrinks at runtime, it offloads or skips layers intelligently, and it exits computation early when predictions stabilize across timesteps. This works because SNN dynamics are redundant—after several timesteps, neuron firing patterns converge and adding more timesteps yields minimal new information, so early exit cuts computation without losing accuracy. By slicing layers fine-grained enough to fit available RAM and scheduling memory-heavy layers when free space peaks, the system keeps all useful computation on-device. The payoff is deploying energy-efficient neuromorphic sensing on phones and edge sensors without cloud connectivity, enabling privacy-preserving real-time inference for IoT applications.

UMCFS selects informative features from data spanning multiple sources, where the core challenge is that sources contain different samples but share features, and naive feature selection mistakes spurious correlations (caused by confounding factors) for true relationships. The method learns weights that balance data across sources (so no source dominates), then identifies which features have causal influence by separating shared global importance from source-specific variation. This works because true causal features appear consistently across sources as global importance, while spurious correlations are source-specific artifacts—confounding factors corrupt differently in each domain. By enforcing domain balance and explicitly segmenting global from local importance, the algorithm finds features that generalize across sources rather than idiosyncratic matches. The payoff is selecting features that transfer across heterogeneous datasets without label supervision, improving downstream models' robustness and interpretability.

This paper measures whether reasoning-enhancement techniques in language models (chain-of-thought, self-reflection, multi-agent debate) inadvertently amplify unfair or stereotyped outputs. The core question is whether step-by-step reasoning, which improves correctness, also gives the model more opportunity to express latent biases. The method benchmarks models on fairness and stereotype tasks with and without reasoning frameworks, measuring how each technique affects alignment. This works because longer reasoning provides more text surface where biases can leak out—if a model harbors stereotypes, asking it to explain multiple times creates more chances to express them. By comparing reasoning techniques across models and languages, the authors isolate which framings amplify unfairness and which preserve safety. The finding—that verbosity does not automatically improve fairness—highlights that scaling reasoning ability alone is insufficient; fairness-aware prompting must accompany complexity. The payoff is understanding alignment trade-offs so deployment of advanced reasoning does not regress on ethics.

FCUCR recommends items to users in federated settings where user data never leaves their devices, while adapting to changing preferences over time and respecting privacy. The core challenge is that users' interests evolve, older preferences degrade in importance, yet each client trains privately without seeing others' data. The method uses self-distillation to retain historical preferences implicitly (newer model predictions on old data guide the updated model) and transfers representative profiles from similar users to enrich each client's personalization. This works because historical preferences encode stable taste structures even as specific interests shift—distilling the old model preserves these stable patterns while allowing new data to reshape details. Prototype transfer works because users naturally cluster by preference type, and borrowing prototypes from peers exposes a client to diverse examples without violating privacy. The payoff is long-term personalization that improves as users' tastes evolve, achieved without centralizing personal data or synchronizing gradients.

This workshop abstract outlines an emerging intersection of foundation models and federated learning in web research. The core opportunity is combining two complementary technologies: foundation models (general-purpose learners trained at scale) and federated learning (training without centralizing sensitive data). The pairing works because foundation models' broad capabilities can be adapted locally (on devices or edges) where federated learning ensures privacy, and federated training can improve foundation models' robustness across diverse data distributions. Neither alone solves the challenge—foundation models trained centrally risk privacy violations, and federated learning on small local models underutilizes available compute. The workshop convenes researchers to explore this synergy and chart research directions. The payoff is combining the data efficiency and generalization of large models with the privacy and control guarantees of decentralized training, addressing a key tension in deployed web-scale machine learning.
